headline.main: The Case Before the ICJ: Is Israel Committing Genocide in the Gaza Strip?
headline.social: The Case Before the ICJ: Is Israel Committing Genocide in the Gaza Strip?

intro: The UN Genocide Convention came about as a reaction to the Holocaust. Now, Israel is being accused of violating it. International law experts are divided.
text:
Itamar Mann’s grandfather owned a legal practice in Berlin until the Nazis banned him from working. He emigrated to Palestine in 1936, thus escaping the Holocaust – before then spending the rest of his life seeking reparations from Germany for the sufferings of his clients. Itamar Mann’s father worked as a defense attorney in Israel. Itamar Mann himself became an international law expert. The 45-year-old is a professor and teaches at the University of Haifa. He joined a video interview from a garden in the Lichterfelde district of Berlin. He has been in the German capital for the last year on a research grant from the Humboldt Foundation.
It is a sad irony, says Itamar Mann, that here, on German soil – and, as a recent development, as a German citizen – he would utter the following sentence: "I am becoming increasingly convinced that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza." As a person who grew up in Israel and who loves the place, he says, it is a painful thing for him to say. And it was not his original view, even as the first voices began accusing his country of genocide. At first, he saw the war against Hamas in Gaza as a justified response to the terrorist attack of October 7, 2023.
But the more brutal the war became, the greater his doubts grew. He can even identify the precise moment when his view shifted for good: It was February 4, 2025, the day Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Donald Trump in the White House and the U.S. president announced his plan to turn the Gaza Strip into a "Riviera of the Middle East." The idea calls for the complete reconstruction of the region – without the Palestinians, who, in Trump’s vision, would "voluntarily” leave.
After that, Israel continued pursuing the war in incredibly brutal fashion, systematically starving the Palestinians before then introducing a dysfunctional aid distribution system, says Mann. Now, people are shot and killed almost every day as they try to get a bit of rice or flour.
Is Gaza the Next on the List?
Will what’s taking place in Gaza ultimately be seen as the latest catastrophe in a series with the Holocaust and the genocides in Rwanda and Srebrenica? In Rwanda, at least 800,000 people were slaughtered in 1994, most of them belonging to the Tutsi minority. In Srebrenica, Bosnian Serb troops took control of the UN Safe Area in Srebrenica and murdered more than 8,000 people, the majority of them Muslim men and boys.
Rwanda and Srebrenica are the only genocides deemed such by international courts. Will Gaza be the next?
Many supporters of the Palestinians felt from the very first days of the war that Israel was committing genocide. For almost three months, the ugly word bounced around the social media echo chambers and was chanted at demonstrations. South Africa then transformed the accusation into a formal legal complaint, submitting it to the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague on December 29, 2023. The court has jurisdiction over violations of the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.
That step catapulted the word "genocide” into the orbit of international law – and the accusations that had been leveled at Israel became a legal dispute.
Expectations of the proceedings are immense. The one side is hoping that Israel will be found guilty because they want justice for the civilian victims in the Gaza Strip. The other side wants acquittal, believing it was Hamas and not Israel that acted with genocidal intent. And still others are hoping for an answer to the question: What kind of war is this that isn’t just a catastrophe for the people of Gaza, but which has also polarized societies in the U.S. and Europe?
The court, though, works slowly. A verdict will likely only be reached a few years from now. By then, hopefully, the war will have long since ended and the first of the hundreds of thousands of destroyed buildings in Gaza will already be rebuilt.
What, then, is the point? Is it really conceivable that the judges in The Hague will actually find Israel guilty of genocide – in violation of a convention that was established as a reaction to the Holocaust?
Can such a thing really come to pass? Must it come to pass?
Sound Moral and Legal Judgment
Back to Itamar Mann in Berlin. Is it not absurd, Mr. Mann, that Israel is now suspected of committing genocide?
Of course, he says calmly. "Those who have participated in genocide become illegitimate actors and are thus forbidden to speak in the public sphere. And indeed, for some, this is precisely what the accusation is aimed to serve – delegitimizing Israeli and possibly Jewish voices as such." It cannot be ignored, he says, that the accusation of genocide against Israel is frequently cloaked in anti-Semitic rhetoric. "But we cannot allow this to prevent us from making sound moral and legal judgments and calling it genocide when that is what we are seeing take place.”
Many of his colleagues in Israel, though, are having a hard time doing exactly that, Mann says. They see violations, but not genocide. Even those few who maybe believe that Israel’s actions in the Gaza Strip could rise to the level of genocide, have their doubts as to whether it makes political sense to discuss it. "It’s a taboo,” says Mann. And a taboo, he believes, that must be broken.
"One might wonder: What’s happening in Gaza is bad enough, why do we need the official designation of genocide?” says Kai Ambos, before answering the question himself. "Because the other human rights violations do not cover the targeted extermination of an entire group.” There is a reason, he says, that genocide is frequently referred to as the "crime of crimes.”
Ambos, 60, is a professor at the University of Göttingen and was one of the first international law experts in Germany to speak of a possible genocide in Gaza. "In summary, the dynamics of the conflict as a whole now speak more for genocide than against it,” he and his colleague Stefanie Bock recently wrote in the Deutsche Richterzeitung, a German law journal. Every word of their piece was chosen with care. But the statement packs a punch. Ambos also says that he is breaking a taboo.
Initially, he also rejected the accusations of genocide. In contrast to Itamar Mann, though, he is unable to pinpoint the precise moment of his conversion. It was, he says, "a gradual process.” And "at some point, you have to say: It all amounts to the destruction of the Palestinians as a group.”
The Key Is Genocidal Intent
Many international law experts agree that the ICJ has jurisdiction in this case, and that the Palestinians in Gaza are considered a protected group as defined in the Genocide Convention. Furthermore, after almost two years of war, there is very little doubt in the international law community that Israel has committed war crimes and crimes against humanity, defined as systematic attacks against the Palestinian civilian population. But multiple war crimes do not simply add up to genocide.
Genocide – this is central to its definition – is the product of intent. Without genocidal intent, there is no genocide. And this intent, here is where it gets complicated, must be extremely specific. Palestinians must have been killed by Israel with the objective of destroying them as a group "in whole or in part,” as the Convention reads.
This intent is clearest when an extermination plan exists, such as in the Nazi’s Wannsee Protocol from 1942 on the "final solution of the Jewish question.” If there is no blueprint and no clear orders, genocidal intent must be proven by evidence. The judges of the ICJ have set a high hurdle for that evidence: Genocidal intent must be the "only reasonable inference” in light of the evidence. That was the bar used in the judgment against Serbia and Montenegro in 2007 – where the judges ruled that it had not been met. As such, the court did not rule that Serbia’s war on the whole was genocide, but it did find that the massacre in Srebrenica met that standard.
Ambos, the international law expert, says that he doesn’t believe the Israeli government has a plan for the extermination of the Palestinians. As such, he says, in order to determine whether genocidal intent exists or not, judges must examine Israeli attacks, acts of war and the blockading of aid goods in addition to internal government resolutions and statements from Israeli politicians and military officials. Statements in which the Palestinians have been described as "human animals,” for example, or those calling for starvation and destruction.
They must look at all the incriminating evidence. And all the exculpatory evidence. A trial by circumstantial evidence, on the highest level. And in the end, even in international law, the benefit of the doubt goes to the accused.
The "Only Reasonable Inference”
Ambos believes that accusations of genocide are supported by the fact that the war doesn’t seem to be following any kind of military purpose, the hostages aren’t being freed. On top of that comes the destruction of the entire civilian infrastructure, the attacks on civilians and the blockade of humanitarian aid goods. But he can also see the counterarguments. "Every measure aimed at protecting the group, even if is a failed method like the distribution of aid goods through the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation, is an argument against genocide.” A ceasefire, he says, could be seen in a similar way. Ambos admits that he struggles with this ambivalence.
International law expert Janina Dill, 42, a professor at Oxford, sees it differently. "Genocide does not have to be fully completed,” she says. Intent can change, a ceasefire doesn’t automatically nullify the accusations. The number of victims, she says, is not the only determining factor.
For example, the Higher Regional Court in Frankfurt convicted a former Islamic State fighter of genocide despite him being responsible for killing just a single Yazidi woman. Yet 60,000 dead Palestinians might not amount to genocide? That is difficult to understand. But it may nevertheless be correct. Genocide, after all, is also a story of misunderstandings.
Contributing to those misunderstandings is the recognition of various genocides by governments and parliaments. Germany, for example, has officially determined that the crimes committed against the Armenians during World War I, the killings of the Herero and Nama in the colony of German South West Africa (now Namibia) in the early 20th century and the mass murders of Yazidis in Iraq in the 2010s were all instances of genocide. Other countries have declared the crimes committed by China against the Uighurs and the slaughter perpetrated by the Khmer Rouge in Cambodia to constitute genocide. U.S. President Donald Trump has recently begun speaking of a genocide against white citizens of South Africa.
Dill says she has been conducting research into war crimes for 15 years. In Gaza, she sees a clear pattern of disproportionate attacks by the Israeli army that raise a reasonable suspicion of war crimes. "But genocide is not simply a series of war crimes. It is not always visible to the naked eye.”
In one sense, the verdict genocide for Dill is the product of a legal process. At the end of that process must be a finding that genocidal intent is attributable to a state, and not just to individuals, and that this is the "only reasonable inference” that can be drawn from the evidence.
That doesn’t mean for her that there couldn’t also be other motives for the war. "Israel points out that it is defending its legitimate security interests, essentially saying: We cannot be committing genocide.” But, Dill says, that is a misunderstanding. More than one intent may guide action. "For a verdict, there can, however, be no reasonable interpretation of the actions that does not involve genocidal intent.” The more motives are at play, the harder it becomes to show genocidal intent. Overall, she says, the hurdle for showing genocide is "very, very high.”
Still, she says something quite surprising in conclusion: "I can imagine the ICJ ultimately ruling: Yes, it is genocide.” She was careful for quite some time, she says, but her views have changed in recent months. "What is happening in Gaza isn’t all that far off from the historical archetype of genocide.”
The Case in Myanmar
Plus, international law is continuing to develop. It depends on interpretations, and they can change. As it currently stands, experts are critical of the fact that according to existing jurisprudence, it is almost impossible to convict a state of genocide. More and more countries are therefore calling for an expansion of the criteria for genocide.
Germany and other countries, for example, intervened in the ongoing case at the ICJ against Myanmar which was filed in 2019, in which that country’s military dictatorship stands accused of committing genocide against the Rohingya minority. In that intervention, Berlin argued that the ICJ should lower its high threshold when it comes to proof of genocidal intent. Forced displacement and violence against children, Germany and the other countries joining the intervention argued, should be given particularly strong consideration.
A verdict on Myanmar could come as soon as next year. Should the judges follow the view submitted by Germany and the others, the criteria would also have to be applied to the proceedings against Israel. And that would make a conviction more likely: According to Palestinian authorities, more than 17,000 children have been killed in Gaza, and most of the coastal strip’s residents have been displaced numerous times.
Stefan Talmon is among those who believe that such a lowering of the standards for proving genocide would be a dangerous development. He teaches at the University of Bonn and is currently in Oxford on a sabbatical. Genocide – or, as he says, "all the awful things” – has been his academic focus for almost 20 years. He is convinced that the accusation should never be made lightly. If a country is found to have committed genocide, its citizens will be branded as perpetrators for generations, he points out. As such, he believes, it is correct for the standards to be high.
No Clear Intent
"I was one of the first in Germany to say that Israel was committing war crimes,” Talmon says. "And now, I say: But it falls legally short of genocide. Many people don’t understand that. Am I on the side of the Palestinians or the Israelis?” In the political debate, he says critically, accusations of genocide are used to demonize the other side. For him, the complaint filed at the ICJ by South Africa is an attempt to enforce morality by means of law.
Talmon may have another reason for his position: He is one of Myanmar’s counsel in the ICJ proceedings. As such, he has an interest in a narrow interpretation of the Genocide Convention.
Of himself, he says he is a "black letter lawyer,” one who hews strictly to precedent and shies away from adopting legal interpretations based on what the law might be in the future. As such, he strongly believes: "It will not be possible to prove genocide in Gaza in the legal sense.”
The evidence must be convincing, he says, and it is only convincing if it does not allow for any other reasonable inference than genocidal intent. Ethnic cleansing, vengeance and displacement, though, are other possible inferences from Israel’s actions – all of them horrible enough, but not clear evidence of genocide.
Just 24 Hours to Prove Genocide
He compares it with a murder trial. The authorities have the bloody murder weapon in their possession, DNA samples, a suspect – and then, on the strength of this evidence, they must convict him. But a conviction will only come if the evidence allows for no other conclusion than guilt. "Ultimately, it works the same at the ICJ,” says Talmon. The problem, though, is just that the ICJ judges don’t have several months to examine the evidence, he says.
He says he has just come from a meeting on scheduling an upcoming genocide hearing at the ICJ. "Eight half-days. That amounts to 24 hours to prove whether a genocide took place or not.” He laughs out loud. Completely impossible. The situation will likely be similar in the Gaza proceedings, he says. "The burden of proof is on South Africa. And all Israel has to do is demonstrate that the evidence allows for other reasonable inferences.”
Israel’s defense could argue, for example, that the destruction was the consequence of security considerations. Instead of taking buildings in street fighting or clearing them of potential booby traps, they chose to simply bomb them. Disproportionate, to be sure, "but that doesn’t mean they acted with the intention of destroying the Palestinians as a group.”
Talmon’s prediction is clear: "According to current jurisprudence, South Africa will lose this case.” At least when it comes to the main claim of genocide. Judges could uphold some additional claims in the South African complaint, such as the one accusing Israel of not preventing incitement to commit genocide. There are many international law experts who take a similar view.
Ultimately, it depends on the 17 judges. Their convictions, their backgrounds, the weight they give to human rights. And on what happens in Gaza. What media outlets report and the findings of the UN and other international organizations. It is impossible to predict how the judges might decide a few years from now – in part because only a simple majority of nine votes is required.
Should the vote ultimately decide against genocide, headlines would possibly read: "Israel Found Not Guilty.” And that – Dill, Ambos, Mann and Talmon all agree – wouldn’t just be fatal, it would also be wrong.
"Few morel consequences follow from a judgment that a state did not commit genocide during the war,” says Janina Dill. The war crimes took place, nonetheless. It is therefore perhaps not so important what the court might one day decide. Rather, the important part is that this debate takes place now.
